1.note: The author is using the term **sons** to mean “descendants.” (This verse seems intended to list five generations of Judah’s descendants in order to provide an introductory summary for verses 2–23.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Judah]

Given the apparent purpose of this verse, many interpreters consider the name **Carmi** here to refer to the Caleb who was the son of Hezron and the father of Hur 2:18–19. Carmi may be an alternative name for Caleb, like Chelubai in 2:9, or it may be the result of a copyist’s mistake. Since no ancient manuscripts or versions have the name Caleb here, we encourage you to use the name Carmi in your translation, but you could explain the apparent purpose of this verse in a footnote.

3.note: The author uses the singular term **father** even though he then names three men. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a plural term here and in similar instances in the book. Alternate translation: [And these were the fathers of Etam]

Since **Etam** is the name of a settlement (as 4:32 indicates), the author is using the term **father** to mean “founder” or “leader.” The meaning of “father” is the same in the next two verses. Alternate translation: [And these were the founders of Etam] or [And these were the leaders of Etam]

7.note: The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) and another ancient version read “Izhar.” That may have been the original reading, as that was a much more common name in this culture. The Hebrew letter “I” is very similar to the letter that represents the word **and** here, and copyists could have mistaken one letter for the other. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

8.note: Since **Aharhel** was the **son** of **Harum**, it is not literally true that Coz **fathered** him and the **clans** that descended from him. The author means that he was the ancestor of Aharhel. Alternate translation: [and who was the ancestor of the clans of Aharhel]

9.note: The expression **was honored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Now people honored Jabez more than his brothers]

Since the book does not introduce **Jabez** in any other way, many interpreters understand the term **brothers** to refer to the sons of Helah listed in the two preceding verses. This would mean that Jabez was a descendant of Judah through Hezron. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could suggest this possible explanation in a footnote.
It might seem that the expression **called his name** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [named him]

The author assumes that readers will know, as the context also indicates, that the name **Jabez** means “he causes pain.” You could indicate this in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

See the discussion of the term **saying** in the Introduction to 1 Chronicles. In contexts such as this, it introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly, here, in the next verse, or in the other instances in this book.

10.q: אִם־בָּרֵ֨ךְ תְּבָרֲכֵ֜⁠נִי וְ⁠הִרְבִּ֤יתָ אֶת־גְּבוּלִ⁠י֙ וְ⁠הָיְתָ֤ה יָדְ⁠ךָ֙ עִמִּ֔⁠י וְ⁠עָשִׂ֥יתָ מֵּ⁠רָעָ֖ה לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֣י עָצְבִּ֑⁠י
10.note: Following the custom of his culture, Jabez is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [If blessing, you would bless me, and you would enlarge my border, and your hand would be with me, and you would act not {in} harm, so as not to pain me, then I would praise you and always be thankful]

Jabez is repeating forms of the verb **bless** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you would surely bless me]

Here the term **border** represents “territory.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my territory] or [my land holdings]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your power would be with me]

Jabez is using **would be with me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “would help me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you would use your power to help me]

The author is speaking as if what Jabez **asked** God to do were an object that God **brought** to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And God did what he asked]

12.note: The expression **Ir Nahash** could be the name of a person, or it could mean “the city of Nahash.” In that case, “father” would mean “founder.” Alternate translation: [the founder of the city of Nahash]

13.note: Some manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation read “Hathath and Meonothai.” That may have been the original reading, since the next verse mentions Meonothai. You may wish to follow this reading in your translation, particularly if there is a major translation in your area and it does so. Alternate translation: [Hathath and Meonothai]

14.note: The author assumes that readers will understand that he is explaining how **Ge Harashim**, which means “The Valley of the Craftsmen,” got its name. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [which got that name because the people who lived there were craftsmen]

17.q: וּ⁠בֶן־עֶזְרָ֔ה יֶ֥תֶר וּ⁠מֶ֖רֶד וְ⁠עֵ֣פֶר וְ⁠יָל֑וֹן וַ⁠תַּ֨הַר֙ אֶת־מִרְיָ֣ם וְ⁠אֶת־שַׁמַּ֔י וְ⁠אֶת־יִשְׁבָּ֖ח אֲבִ֥י אֶשְׁתְּמֹֽעַ וְ⁠אִשְׁתּ֣⁠וֹ הַ⁠יְהֻדִיָּ֗ה יָלְדָ֞ה אֶת־יֶ֨רֶד אֲבִ֤י גְדוֹר֙ וְ⁠אֶת־חֶ֨בֶר֙ אֲבִ֣י שׂוֹכ֔וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־יְקֽוּתִיאֵ֖ל אֲבִ֣י זָנ֑וֹחַ וְ⁠אֵ֗לֶּה בְּנֵי֙ בִּתְיָ֣ה בַת־פַּרְעֹ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר לָקַ֖ח מָֽרֶד
17.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine 4:17 and 4:18 into a verse bridge in order to clarify who the mothers of Mered’s children were. Alternate translation: [And the sons of Ezrah: Jether and Mered and Epher and Jalon. And Mered took Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, and these were her sons: she conceived Miriam and Shammai and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa. And his Judahitess wife bore Jered, the father of Gedor, and Heber, the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel, the father of Zanoah.]

21.note: The author is using the term **house** to mean people descended from a particular ancestor, and in this context, it describes how they lived and worked together at a particular trade. (From ancient times, certain families among the Israelites did specific kinds of work, passing their expertise down through the generations.) Alternate translation: [the guild of linen workers]

33.note: The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) and the parallel passage in Joshua 19:8 read “Baalath.” That may have been the original reading, and you may wish to use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [Baalath]

34.q: וּ⁠מְשׁוֹבָ֣ב וְ⁠יַמְלֵ֔ךְ וְ⁠יוֹשָׁ֖ה בֶּן אֲמַצְיָֽה וְ⁠יוֹאֵ֑ל וְ⁠יֵהוּא֙ בֶּן־י֣וֹשִׁבְיָ֔ה בֶּן־שְׂרָיָ֖ה בֶּן־עֲשִׂיאֵֽל וְ⁠אֶלְיוֹעֵינַ֡י וְֽ⁠יַעֲקֹ֡בָה וִ֠⁠ישׁוֹחָיָה וַ⁠עֲשָׂיָ֧ה וַ⁠עֲדִיאֵ֛ל וִ⁠ישִׂימִאֵ֖ל וּ⁠בְנָיָֽה וְ⁠זִיזָ֨א בֶן־שִׁפְעִ֧י בֶן־אַלּ֛וֹן בֶּן־יְדָיָ֥ה בֶן־שִׁמְרִ֖י בֶּן־שְׁמַֽעְיָֽה אֵ֚לֶּה הַ⁠בָּאִ֣ים בְּ⁠שֵׁמ֔וֹת נְשִׂיאִ֖ים בְּ⁠מִשְׁפְּחוֹתָ֑⁠ם וּ⁠בֵית֙ אֲב֣וֹתֵי⁠הֶ֔ם פָּרְצ֖וּ לָ⁠רֽוֹב
34.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine 4:34–38 into a verse bridge in order to explain that this is a list of clan leaders before listing all of the names in these verses. This would also put the reason (these families became large) before the result (there were many clan leaders in them). The UST models one way to do this.

38.note: The author is using **the house of their fathers** as a common expression of his culture to describe extended families, comprising three or four generations, led by a man who was the father, grandfather, or great-grandfather of the family members. The household also included servants. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their extended families] or [their clans]

The author is speaking as if these extended families actually **broke through** some barrier in order to become very large. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [increased greatly] or [became very large]

40.note: The author is using **broad of two hands** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the land was open on both sides, in other words, it was not a valley confined within mountains. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was an open plain]

The author is using the dual of the word “hand.” He is not using the number two and the plural of “hand.” Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. If your language has a dual form, it would be appropriate to use it here.

40.q: וְ⁠שֹׁקֶ֖טֶת וּ⁠שְׁלֵוָ֑ה כִּ֣י מִן־חָ֔ם הַ⁠יֹּשְׁבִ֥ים שָׁ֖ם לְ⁠פָנִֽים
40.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and, since descendants of Ham had been living there before they came, it was quiet and peaceful]

The terms **quiet** and **peaceful** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very peaceful]

The author is using the expression **to their faces** to mean “before them” or “previous to their arrival.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before they came]

41.note: The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And these men whose names appear in the list above came]

The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the time when **Hezekiah** was the king of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during the reign of Hezekiah]
See the discussion of the term “struck” in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [and they attacked]

Here, the **tents** of these descendants of Ham represent their entire “settlements.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their settlements]

The author is using the term **found** in a way characteristic of his language and culture to mean that these **Meunites**, members of a different people group from the descendants of Ham, could be found in the valley of Gedor, that is, they were there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who were living among them]
See the discussion of the phrase **to this day** in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [And they devoted them, and those groups never lived there again]
See how you translated the term “devoted” in 2:7. Alternate translation: [And they destroyed them completely]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because pasture for their flock was there, they dwelled in their place]

42.note: The author is speaking as if these *500** Simeonites were a body or bodies and these four **sons of Ishi** were actually **heads**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their leaders]

43.note: See the discussion of the term “struck” in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [and they killed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of an **escape**, you could express the same idea in another way. The UST models one way to do that.
See the discussion of the phrase **to this day** in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [and they settled there permanently]
